extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of political philosophy and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Full-text Wikisource edition of John Stuart Mill's essay On Liberty (1859), presenting principles and standards about the relationship between individual liberty and political authority. Useful for readers studying limits to state power, individuality, and the dangers of majority tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute and essential importance of human development in its richest diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The grand, leading principle, towards which every argument unfolded in these pages directly converges, is the absolute and essential importance of human development in its richest diversity." (quotation attributed to the work as central principle)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the guiding principle of the essay toward which Mill's arguments converge; frames evaluation of authority vs individual freedom in terms of promoting diverse human development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three basic liberties of individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: "Among the standards proposed are Mill's three basic liberties of individuals" (summary statement on the page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named as one of Mill's explicit standards for the relationship between authority and liberty; the page references these liberties as foundational constraints on state interference (the full text of the essay contains the detailed exposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three legitimate objections to government intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: "Among the standards proposed are ... his three legitimate objections to government intervention" (summary statement on the page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as Mill's criteria limiting when government interference may be justified; the page signals these objections as part of Mill's standards though their full elaboration appears in the essay chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two maxims regarding the relationship of the individual to society
rubrics_metrics.description: "Among the standards proposed are ... his two maxims regarding the relationship of the individual to society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referred to as explicit maxims guiding how individuals and society should interact; the page notes these as part of the work's prescriptive framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of individuality as prerequisite to higher pleasures (summum bonum)
rubrics_metrics.description: "He emphasized the importance of individuality, which he considered a prerequisite to the higher pleasures—the summum bonum of utilitarianism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States Mill's evaluative criterion that individuality is essential to achieving higher forms of human happiness; supports arguments against uniform social conformity and excessive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of the danger of 'tyranny of the majority' under democratic ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: "Furthermore, Mill asserted that democratic ideals may result in the tyranny of the majority."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a normative warning and evaluative standard: democratic processes do not by themselves justify suppression of minority individuality; policy and authority should be assessed for risk of majority despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to the authority of society over the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: (Chapter title) "Of the limits to the authority of society over the individual."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit thematic criterion: the essay develops standards for when society may legitimately impose on individual actions and opinions; functions as an organizing rubric for assessing permissibility of social or legal constraints.
